# Grantha Heritage Tracker: grouping old Indian books by subject without labels

Problem SIH26096 · Section K3P24XC · CO2 & CO3 · Units III & IV · every number from the result files (`reports/deliverable_facts.json`, `reports/features/*.json`)

## 1. Data and scale (Rubric Column 1)

**Q 1.1. Where does the dataset come from, and how big is it?**

15,288 books from the Digital Library of India scans on the Internet Archive, in 8 languages; 13,358 (87.4%) pass the usability gate.

- **Harvest:** a fleet of Google Cloud VMs, one per language (Kannada and Tamil shared one), downloading single pages, never whole PDFs. 77,634 pages were read with Tesseract.
- **Per language (usable of harvested):** English 1,976 of 2,000; Bengali 1,930 of 2,000; Gujarati 1,886 of 2,000; Hindi 1,806 of 2,000; Sanskrit 1,562 of 2,000; Kannada 1,460 of 1,608; Tamil 1,416 of 1,766; Telugu 1,322 of 1,914.

*If an examiner asks: Why not NDLI directly?* NDLI aggregates catalogue records and has no bulk API; the Digital Library of India scans are the files behind many of its records.

**Q 1.2. What is the usability gate, and how many books fail it?**

Word-weighted mean OCR confidence of at least 50 and at least 100 clean tokens. 1,930 books (12.6%) fail.

> usable = (mean_conf ≥ 50) ∧ (clean_tokens ≥ 100) · usable 13,358 · excluded 1,930

*If an examiner asks: Why drop books?* Gibberish OCR creates false closeness between unrelated books. Excluded books stay in the database, flagged, so the decision can be revisited.

*If an examiner asks: Does the gate bias the corpus?* Yes, towards readable scans: Telugu keeps only 69% of its books while English keeps almost all. The results describe readable books, and we say so.

**Q 1.3. How are books split for evaluation?**

By a hash of each book's identifier: 60% train, 20% validation, 20% test, the same for a book forever.

> train 8,129 · validation 2,638 · test 2,591

- Every fitting step (stopwords, PCA, centring, clustering, DBSCAN eps, the edition threshold) sees the train books only.
- An earlier version shuffled the whole corpus; when the corpus grew, held-out books became training books. The hash fixes that, and the change is logged as a deviation in `docs/evaluation_log.md`.

## 2. Preprocessing and vectors (Rubric Column 1)

**Q 2.1. How was OCR done, and which text is embedded?**

Tesseract 5 LSTM (--oem 1 --psm 3) with orientation and script detection; if the detected script disagrees with the catalogue, both models read the page and the more confident one wins.

- This run embeds whole-book text: the archive's own OCR for 12,263 books (10,581 from hOCR, 1,682 from DjVu text), and our five Tesseract pages for the 1,095 books with no archive text.
- Our own Tesseract pages still measure OCR quality for the usability gate.

**Q 2.2. Which variables were kept or dropped?**

Kept: text, script, year (median-imputed plus a missing flag), log pages, OCR confidence, log tokens. Dropped: scanning centre and source library (provenance leakage), subject field, free-text fields.

- Numeric fields are standardised so year (hundreds) does not outweigh confidence (tens); script is one-hot encoded. Adding these fields to the text vectors is tested separately (`reports/study/sensitivity.json`); the final groups use the text alone.

**Q 2.3. How are books turned into vectors, and why centre by language?**

Vertex AI Multilingual embeddings (text-multilingual-embedding-002, 768-d): up to 10 evenly spaced 64-word chunks per book, averaged; each language's mean vector subtracted; PCA to 100 dims.

> μℓ = mean of the train books in language ℓ;  x̃ = (x − μℓ(x)) / ‖x − μℓ(x)‖

- On the 8,129 train books, before centring, groups follow script (NMI 0.642) and 97.3% of each book's 10 nearest neighbours share its script. After centring: NMI 0.065, and 62.8%.

*If an examiner asks: Why is centring the key step?* Without it the strongest signal in a multilingual vector is the language itself, so the groups are language piles we already knew. Removing each language's average is what lets subject show.

*If an examiner asks: Was the encoder chosen by a test?* The pre-registered encoder comparison (LaBSE embeddings, IndicSBERT embeddings, BGE-M3 embeddings, Gemini embeddings) ran on the earlier, smaller study; centring helped every one of them. Vertex AI Multilingual embeddings was a team decision and was not in that comparison. We say so on the deck.

## 3. Hierarchical clustering (Unit III, Rubric Column 2)

**Q 3.1. Compare the linkages and distances.**

The grid runs Ward, average and complete linkage for k from 2 to 15 on the train books. Single linkage chains books one by one, so it cannot give topic groups. In the distance study euclidean won 3 comparisons and Manhattan 1.

| Linkage | Merges by | Behaviour here |
|---|---|---|
| Ward | least increase in within-group variance | compact groups of similar size |
| Complete | largest pairwise distance | sensitive to outlying books |
| Average | mean pairwise distance | between the two |
| Single | smallest pairwise distance | chains books one by one; unusable for topics |

**Q 3.2. How was the final setting chosen?**

By a rule fixed before any results, on the train books: ward linkage, euclidean, k = 3. No setting met the rule, so the pre-registered fallback applied.

> train books: silhouette 0.038 · script NMI 0.017 · bootstrap ARI 0.36;  all usable books: silhouette 0.035 · script NMI 0.019 · bootstrap ARI 0.26

- Rule: highest silhouette among feature sets and valid settings whose groups follow script with NMI <= 0.5 and whose median bootstrap ARI >= 0.5. Fallback if nothing passes: the setting with the lowest script NMI, reported as a rule failure.

*If an examiner asks: Why is silhouette so low?* Books on one subject vary a lot in vocabulary, so groups overlap; silhouette near zero is common for text. Even within one script it stays low (weighted mean 0.050). We judge the groups by held-out subject accuracy instead.

*If an examiner asks: Is k = 3 too few for a library?* Yes, the groups are broad shelves. The rule fell back to k = 3, and we report that rather than pick a larger k by eye.

**Q 3.3. How stable are the groups (target T3)?**

Not stable enough. On train books the median bootstrap ARI is 0.36 against a target of 0.60: not met. On all usable books it is 0.26, with most re-runs between 0.21 and 0.40 (20 resamples of 80%).

- Neighbouring cuts of the same tree agree with the k = 3 cut (k = 2: ARI 0.79; k = 4: ARI 0.81), so the choice of k is not what moves the groups; resampling the books is.
- Refitting on the 8,099 high-confidence books (60.6%) agrees with the full grouping at ARI 0.35 only.

*If an examiner asks: So are the groups real?* They carry some subject signal (next section), but their boundaries shift between samples. We present them as a navigation aid, not a catalogue.

## 4. DBSCAN (Unit IV, Rubric Column 2)

**Q 4.1. How were eps and MinPts chosen, and what does noise mean?**

Sorted k-distance curves set the eps range (0.681 to 1.061); with MinPts 5, 10, 15, 20, 24 settings were run, and the best silhouette among valid ones is eps 0.866, MinPts 15: 2 clusters, 30.7% noise.

- Noise (-1) = a book with fewer than MinPts neighbours within eps, and not near a core book.
- Agreement with the hierarchical groups on non-noise books: ARI 0.0004, no agreement.
- HDBSCAN as a check: 2 clusters with 94.1% of books noise.

*If an examiner asks: Why is the catalogue hierarchical, not DBSCAN?* It assigns every book; DBSCAN's verdict is shown next to it in the app as 'in a dense region' or 'noise'.

*If an examiner asks: DBSCAN is steadier. Why not use it?* Its bootstrap ARI is 0.86, but it leaves 30.7% of books unassigned, finds only 2 clusters, and those do not match the hierarchical groups. A steady split into two dense regions says little about subject.

## 5. PCA (CO3, Rubric Column 2)

**Q 5.1. What does PCA do here, and how much variance is kept?**

PCA reduces 768 → 100 dims for clustering (keeps 78.6%); for display, PC1 11.6% and PC2 8.7% of the 100-d variance.

> Σ = (1/N) XᵀX on centred X; Σ vᵢ = λᵢ vᵢ; share of PC i = λᵢ / Σλ

*If an examiner asks: Only about a fifth of the variance in 2D?* Topics spread over many directions, so a 2D view always shows overlap that the full space does not have. We use PCA rather than t-SNE or UMAP because it does not invent gaps.

## 6. Evaluation (Rubric Column 3)

**Q 6.1. How did you check that the groups mean something (target T2)?**

On 117 labelled test books, each group's majority subject is right 53.0% of the time (95% CI 43.6% to 61.5%), against 38.5% for guessing from the script alone and 30.8% for always guessing the most common subject: +14.5 points over the best simple guess (95% CI +5.1 to +24.8), p = 0.0005 from 2,000 label shuffles. Target +10 points: met.

| Target (fixed in advance) | Validation | Test | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| T1: a page lands with its own book (≥ 80%) | 75.8% | 75.2% | not met |
| T2: subject gain over best simple guess (≥ +10 points) | +4.2 | +14.5 | met |
| T3: bootstrap ARI on train books (≥ 0.60) | 0.36 | 0.36 | not met |

- Test numbers were measured once, after every choice was made on train and validation books.
- Validation books: 45.8% vs 41.7% for the script guess, +4.2 points (95% CI -6.7 to +14.2, p = 0.0025) on 120 books: below the target.
- Groups are named from 351 labelled train books. Labels come from titles, catalogue fields and an OCR snippet, made with an AI assistant for the team to spot-check; they never form or choose groups.

*If an examiner asks: Is this supervised?* No. Clustering never sees a label; labels only measure the groups afterwards.

*If an examiner asks: Validation says +4.2 and test says +14.5. Which is true?* Both are measurements on just over a hundred labelled books each, so both are noisy: the intervals overlap (validation -6.7 to +14.2, test +5.1 to +24.8). The plan judges the target on the test split, measured once, so we report T2 as met, but the test interval reaches below +10 and we do not claim the gain is reliably that large.

**Q 6.2. Does a single new page land with its own book (target T1)?**

75.2% of single test pages land in their own book's group (95% CI 74.1% to 76.3%), against 35.9% by chance. Target 80%: not met.

- 2,362 test books; the app abstained on 2.6% of pages.
- Counting a page as right when its book's group is among its tags (up to 3) gives 85.7%; that is a looser measure, not the target.

*If an examiner asks: Why does a page miss its book's group a quarter of the time?* One page is a small sample of a book, and the groups overlap heavily (silhouette near zero), so a page near a boundary can fall on either side. The app shows the runner-up group and its evidence for that reason.

**Q 6.3. Do the groups match the librarians' catalogue classes?**

No. As an exploratory check on 1,168 test books with a mappable class code, the groups are right 47.8% of the time against 51.8% for guessing from the script: -4.0 points (95% CI -5.2 to -2.9).

- Every group's majority class is language and literature, so the 3 groups cannot separate the catalogue's main classes; NMI between groups and classes is 0.088.
- This check was exploratory in the plan; we report it because it cuts against the headline.

## 7. Tools for the archivist (Rubric Column 3)

**Q 7.1. How good is the class suggestion for an uncatalogued book?**

On 1,168 held-out books with a catalogue class, the top suggestion is the book's own class 58.6% of the time (95% CI 55.8% to 61.5%), against 47.8% for always suggesting the most common class and 51.8% for guessing from the script. The right class is among the top three 91.6% of the time (95% CI 90.1% to 93.1%).

- Method: a distance-weighted vote of the 25 nearest of 3,559 classed train books; nothing is fitted on the held-out books.
- No simple-guess baseline was computed for top-three, so that number stands alone.

*If an examiner asks: Why does the suggestion beat the simple guesses on catalogue classes when the groups do not?* The groups are three broad shelves; the suggestion uses a book's own nearest classed neighbours, which is a much finer signal.

**Q 7.2. Does the tool find related books in other scripts?**

Among each train book's 10 nearest neighbours (8,129 books), 37.2% are in another script after centring, against 2.7% before.

- This shows that books in other scripts now reach the neighbour list; it does not by itself show they share the subject. The deck's example is one recorded answer, not an evaluation.

**Q 7.3. How well does the edition finder work?**

Precision 1.00 and recall 36.4% (95% CI 8.3% to 66.7%), on only 11 held-out edition groups among 2,591 test books.

- The distance threshold (0.0447) is calibrated on train books only.
- An edition counts only when the normalised title and author match exactly, so transliterated or translated editions are not counted as found or missed.

*If an examiner asks: How sure are you of that recall?* Not sure at all. With 11 groups the 95% interval runs from 8.3% to 66.7%. The precision interval is 1.00 to 1.00 only because every candidate in this tiny sample was right; that does not make precision certain. It needs many more held-out groups before we can quote a recall.

**Q 7.4. Does scan triage predict which books need re-OCR?**

No. Its score ranks books against 'our OCR agrees with the archive's OCR less than the median' with an AUC of 0.499 (95% CI 0.452 to 0.546) on 341 books: no better than chance.

- The rules reuse the usability gate's thresholds (confidence below 50, fewer than 100 words) plus DBSCAN noise; their weights (low_conf 0.5, few_tokens 0.3, dbscan_noise 0.2) are design choices, not fitted.

*If an examiner asks: Your triage AUC is 0.50. Why keep it?* As a check it failed, and we report it that way. The verdicts only restate the gate's own rules (why a book was flagged), which is still useful to read, but the score must not be read as a prediction of OCR disagreement.

## 8. Groups and limits (Rubric Column 3)

**Q 8.1. What are the groups?**

3 groups, each named by the majority subject of its labelled train books; every group mixes all 8 languages, and no language holds more than 22% of any group.

| Group | Books | Majority subject | Largest languages |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group 1 | 6,152 | literature | eng 19%, ben 16%, hin 13% |
| Group 2 | 1,714 | religion and philosophy | hin 22%, san 19%, guj 18% |
| Group 3 | 5,492 | religion and philosophy | eng 14%, guj 14%, tam 14% |

**Q 8.2. What are the limits, and how does the app behave responsibly?**

1 of 3 targets met. Page agreement and stability missed; the groups are broad and do not match the catalogue's classes; scan triage is no better than chance; the edition finder is barely tested; labels are AI-assisted; OCR quality is uneven by language; the encoder is an online Google service.

- The app abstains below 20 readable words and cautions when OCR confidence is below 50 or a page has fewer than 100 words, the same bars the archive books passed.
- Every answer lists the five nearest archive books, how far the page is from its group's centre relative to the group's own spread, and DBSCAN's verdict.
- Checking a page sends its text to Google to be embedded.
